title: Package code downloads and executes code
why: The package's own JavaScript, which runs when your app imports it, starts a downloader (curl, wget, PowerShell) or evaluates data fetched from the network. Install-script checks never see this.
fix: Do not ship it: remove the package or pin a version without this code, and check whether the code already ran (safe-install why <pkg> shows what pulls it in).

title: Package code sends credentials over the network
why: The package's code reads credentials (~/.ssh, ~/.npmrc, cloud configs, token variables) right next to a network send: the shape of credential theft.
fix: Remove the package. If your app or tests imported it, rotate the credentials it could reach.

title: Package code is obfuscated
why: javascript-obfuscator naming, or a large encoded blob passed straight to eval or Function, hides what the code does from review.
fix: Find out why a dependency ships obfuscated code; prefer an alternative unless the publisher explains it.

title: Deprecated or missing version
why: Deprecated versions get no fixes; a version missing from the registry was likely unpublished, sometimes for being malicious.
fix: Upgrade to a supported version.

title: Lockfile hash does not match the registry
why: The tarball your lockfile expects is not the one the registry serves: the lockfile was edited or the package was tampered with.
fix: Do not install. Regenerate the lockfile from a trusted state and find out how it changed.

title: Package downloaded from outside the registry
why: A lockfile entry pointing at another host can serve anything, bypassing the registry.
fix: Make sure the URL is expected (a private mirror); otherwise regenerate the lockfile.

title: Install script connected to the network
why: Seen by the runtime monitor (--monitor, Linux). Some packages download binaries; malware phones home or fetches a payload.
fix: Check the destination is the project's own release host. If not, remove the package and treat the machine as exposed.

title: Install script ran a network tool
why: curl, wget, nc, ssh and similar are how scripts download payloads or exfiltrate data.
fix: Read what was run (shown in full). Approve only if it fetches the project's own artifacts.

title: Install script read credentials
why: Reading ~/.ssh, ~/.npmrc, cloud or browser credentials during install is credential theft.
fix: Assume the secrets are stolen: rotate them, then remove the package.

title: Install script touched a persistence location
why: Writing shell startup files, ~/.ssh, autostart or systemd units, git hooks or system directories lets malware survive the install.
fix: Inspect and restore the file, remove the package. --monitor=kill stops the script after the first such action.

title: Install script wrote outside the project
why: Install scripts normally write only to their own directory, temp and package caches.
fix: Check what was written and why.

title: Blocked by policy
why: Your organization's (or project's) policy lists this package in blockPackages: it must not be installed, and its scripts never run.
fix: Remove the package or replace it. If the block is wrong, change it in the policy that sets it (safe-install shows the organization policy in use).

title: Name imitates a popular package
why: Typosquats (lodahs, expres, re-act) rely on a typo in package.json to get installed instead of the real package.
fix: Check the spelling. If you meant the popular package, fix the name; if this one is intended, verify its repository first.

title: Rarely used package runs install scripts
why: Malware is often published as a new, barely downloaded package whose install script does the damage.
fix: Make sure you know why this package is in your tree and read its script before approving.

title: Version published recently
why: Compromised releases are usually caught and unpublished within days. Waiting minReleaseAge before using a version avoids most of them.
fix: Wait, pin an older version, or exempt a trusted fast-moving package with minReleaseAgeExclude in .safe-install.json.

title: Unusual publisher on a recent release
why: A release published without the provenance its predecessor had, or by someone who never published the package before, is what a stolen token looks like.
fix: Check the package's repository and release notes for this version before using it.

title: Package runs install scripts
why: preinstall/install/postinstall scripts run arbitrary code on your machine during install. Most malicious packages use them.
fix: Read the script. If it is expected (native builds, binary downloads from the project's own release), approve it: safe-install approve <pkg>.

title: Install script downloads and executes code
why: Piping a download into a shell (curl | sh, iwr | iex, encoded PowerShell) runs code nobody reviewed, fetched at install time.
fix: Do not approve. Find out why the package does this; report it to the registry if it looks malicious.

title: Install script evaluates dynamic or encoded code
why: eval, new Function and long encoded blobs are how malware hides its payload from review.
fix: Inspect the decoded code before approving. Legitimate install scripts rarely need this.

title: Install script touches credentials
why: Reading ~/.ssh, ~/.npmrc, cloud credentials or token variables during install is the classic way to steal secrets.
fix: Do not approve unless you understand exactly why the package needs them.

title: Install scripts changed since approval
why: The scripts, or the files they run, differ from what was approved, as happens when a package is compromised.
fix: Review the new scripts, then approve again: safe-install approve <pkg>.

title: Known advisory
why: OSV lists this version as malicious (MAL-…, blocked) or vulnerable. Vulnerabilities count one level below their advisory severity; npm audit covers them in depth.
fix: For a malicious package: remove it and rotate any credentials on machines that installed it. For a vulnerability: upgrade to a fixed version.
